questions.stem: Exact data give $p(0)=1$, $p(1)=2$, $p(2)=5$ and $p(3)=10$. First assume $p$ is a real polynomial of degree at most three: determine it and justify uniqueness. Then remove the degree bound and characterise every real polynomial consistent with the same four data points. State precisely which inference depended on the bound.
questions.answer: For degree at most 3, p(x)=x^2+1; uniqueness follows because the difference of two such polynomials has four distinct zeros but degree at most 3. Without the bound, p=x^2+1+x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)q for arbitrary real polynomial q. The degree bound is exactly what forces q=0.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: what four exact observations do and do not determine
qrt_targets.Y: factor theorem plus the root-count bound
qrt_targets.Z: separate bounded uniqueness from the unrestricted vanishing-factor family
qrt_targets.W: the degree-bound warrant that forces the difference to vanish

questions.stem: A nonzero real polynomial has degree at most four and zeros at $-2$, $0$ and $2$. It changes sign across each of $-2$ and $2$, but has the same nonzero sign on the two sides sufficiently close to $0$. Also $p(1)=-3$. Construct the polynomial, justify the multiplicity information you use, and establish whether these conditions determine it uniquely. These are exact benchmark conditions, not measurements from a graph.
questions.answer: Sign changes at -2 and 2 force odd multiplicities; same nonzero sign across 0 forces an even multiplicity. The degree budget forces multiplicities 1,2,1. Thus p=k(x+2)x^2(x-2), and p(1)=-3 gives k=1; unique.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: what local sign behaviour says about root multiplicity
qrt_targets.Y: odd/even multiplicity sign rules and the degree budget

questions.stem: Find the least possible degree of a real polynomial whose distinct real zeros are exactly $-1$ and $1$, and which satisfies $p(0)=p(2)=1$. Exhibit one such polynomial, verify that it has no other real zeros, and prove that every smaller degree is impossible. You may use continuity of real polynomial functions and the factor theorem. This is an advanced competition extension.
questions.answer: Write p=(x^2-1)g, so g(0)=-1 and g(2)=1/3. Degree 2 is impossible; degree 3 forces a linear g with extra zero 3/2; degree 4 forces a quadratic g that changes sign on (0,2), hence has a real zero there and cannot avoid an extra distinct zero. Degree 5 works: p=(1/3)(x+1)(x-1)^2(x^2-3x+3); the quadratic discriminant is -3.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: why exact values and an exact zero set impose a lower bound
qrt_targets.Y: factor theorem, continuity and quadratic discriminant

questions.stem: For real $a$, consider $F_a(x)=(a-1)x^4+2(a-1)x^3+(a+2)x^2+2(a+2)x$. Develop a complete classification of its degree and number of distinct real zeros as $a$ varies. Identify all exceptional parameter values where the degree drops or zeros coincide, and account for multiplicities at those values. Justify that your cases are exhaustive.
questions.answer: F_a=x(x+2)((a-1)x^2+(a+2)). Degree is 2 at a=1 and 4 otherwise. Extra real roots occur exactly for -2<a<1. Exceptional values are a=-2 (0 has multiplicity 3), a=2/5 (the negative extra root collides with -2, making it double), and a=1 (degree drop). Therefore: a<-2: 2 distinct simple zeros; a=-2: 2 distinct; -2<a<1 except 2/5: 4 distinct simple; a=2/5: 3 distinct; a=1: 2 distinct simple degree2; a>1: 2 distinct simple.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: which parameter events change degree, root existence or coincidence
qrt_targets.Z: derive every critical value then partition parameter space
qrt_targets.W: the exhaustive event set and interval/collision split

questions.stem: An open box is formed by cutting squares of side $x$ cm from the corners of a $10$ cm square sheet and folding the sides up, ignoring thickness. An exact calculation table gives volumes $0$, $64$ and $72$ cubic centimetres at $x=0,1,2$ respectively; $x=0$ denotes the flat limiting configuration. An analyst fits $Q(x)=-28x^2+92x$ to these three entries and treats it as the volume model. Derive the model from the geometry, state the domain for a non-degenerate box, assess the fitted model over that domain, and choose an additional admissible input that discriminates between the two accounts. Explain why matching the recorded entries is insufficient.
questions.answer: Geometry gives V=x(10-2x)^2 on 0<x<5. The fitted Q=-28x^2+92x matches the three recorded rows but Q-V=-4x(x-1)(x-2). At admissible x=4, V=16 while Q=-80. Finite agreement is not a geometric model or an unrestricted identity proof.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: which account is a geometric model and which only interpolates
qrt_targets.Z: derive V, compare Q-V, then test a changed input
qrt_targets.W: the inference that three rows do not identify the model

questions.stem: For real $a$, let $R_a(x)=[x^2-(a+1)x+a]/(x-a)$ with its original domain $x\neq a$. A student cancels a factor and says that every $R_a$ is the same polynomial function on all real numbers, with zero $1$. Determine which parts of that statement hold on the original domains, classify the real zeros as $a$ varies, and describe the polynomial extension separately. Explain why extending a function and preserving its original domain are different operations.
questions.answer: The numerator is (x-a)(x-1), so R_a=x-1 only on x!=a. If a!=1, x=1 is an allowed zero; if a=1 it is excluded and there are no zeros. The polynomial extension x-1 is defined on all reals and always has zero 1; filling the hole changes the function domain.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.Z: cancel on the original domain then classify extension

questions.stem: A real polynomial $p$ has degree at most four, satisfies $p(-x)=p(x)$ for every real $x$, and has $p(1)=p(2)=0$ and $p(0)=4$. Classify the following claims as necessary, possible but not necessary, or impossible under these conditions: its degree is two; it has exactly four distinct real zeros; it also has zero $3$; its leading coefficient is $1$; the data determine a unique polynomial. Justify each verdict. Reassess the claims when the degree bound is removed, while all other conditions are retained.
questions.answer: With degree at most 4, evenness forces roots ±1,±2 and p(0)=4 gives p=(x^2-1)(x^2-4). Thus degree2 impossible, exactly four distinct real zeros necessary, zero3 impossible, leading coefficient1 necessary, and uniqueness necessary. Without the degree bound, p=(x^2-1)(x^2-4)h with even h and h(0)=1; only degree2 remains impossible, while the other bounded conclusions become possible-but-not-necessary or uniqueness becomes false.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: which consequences require the degree bound

questions.stem: Real polynomials $p$ and $q$ each have degree at most three. They agree at $x=-1,0,1$, but $p(2)-q(2)=12$. Characterise every possible difference polynomial, determine $p(3)-q(3)$, and decide whether the evidence identifies either polynomial individually. Use explicit examples to separate uniqueness of a difference from uniqueness of its two components.
questions.answer: d=p-q has degree at most 3 and roots -1,0,1, so d=kx(x^2-1). d(2)=12 gives k=2 and d(3)=48. p and q are not individually identified: choose any cubic-or-less r and set q=r, p=r+d.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.Z: factor the difference then construct distinct decompositions

questions.stem: Characterise all monic real polynomials of degree at most four whose distinct real zeros are exactly $-1$ and $1$ and whose value at zero is $1$. Explain how repeated factors and any remaining quadratic factor affect completeness of your list. Prove both that every item in your list works and that no allowed polynomial has been omitted.
questions.answer: Let multiplicities at 1 and -1 be m,n>=1. With no leftover factor, p(0)=(-1)^m=1, so m is even; degree at most 4 gives (m,n)=(2,1) or (2,2). A leftover monic quadratic can only occur with m=n=1; p(0)=1 then forces constant -1, giving discriminant b^2+4>0 and unwanted real roots. Hence exactly (x-1)^2(x+1) and (x-1)^2(x+1)^2.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: how multiplicities and leftover factors interact with all constraints
qrt_targets.Y: factor theorem and quadratic real-root test
qrt_targets.Z: enumerate cases and eliminate the quadratic remainder

questions.stem: A solver uses four rules: cancellation makes a rational expression a polynomial on all real numbers; the largest printed exponent is always the degree; a degree-$n$ polynomial has exactly $n$ distinct real zeros; agreement at three inputs proves an identity. Develop a qualified decision procedure and apply it to: $A_t(x)=(t-1)x^3+x^2-1$ with real $t$; $B(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ on its original domain; $C(x)=(x-2)^2(x^2+1)$; and the pair $D(x)=x^2+1$, $E(x)=x^2+1+x(x-1)(x-2)$ compared at $x=0,1,2$. State the relevant conditions and valid conclusions in each case, then create one fresh counterexample to an unqualified rule. Preserve the difference between expressions, functions, identities and finite observations.
questions.answer: Cancellation preserves equality only on the original domain; degree is read after simplification and parameter leading-coefficient checks; a nonzero degree-n polynomial has at most n distinct real zeros; finite agreement proves identity only with a suitable degree bound on the difference. A_t has degree3 except t=1, when degree2; B equals x+1 only for x!=1; C has degree4 but one distinct real zero 2 of multiplicity2; D and E agree at 0,1,2 but differ, e.g. by 6 at x=3. Fresh counterexample: (x-3)^2/(x-3) on x!=3.

difficulty.basis: Governed five-component estimate; the intended D4 cohort is not pre-adjudication.

qrt_targets.X: the hidden condition omitted by each shortcut
qrt_targets.Y: domain, simplified degree, root-count and identity bounds
qrt_targets.Z: qualify each rule then apply it
